findings.title: Rotated examples, persistent refusal
findings.claim: In 17:88 the human-jinn coalition cannot bring the Qur'an's likeness; in 17:89 its presentation turns through every example for people, while most still refuse. The following demands keep that response in view as the requested proof forms change.
findings.mechanism: The focus carriers ṣarrafnā, min kull mathal, abā, akthar, and kufuran join a varied and exhaustive address to a measured refusal. The prior failure to reproduce the Qur'an and the later requests for material signs and a self-readable book make the contrast concrete: presentation changes, while refusal remains active. The supplied truth and favor contexts let kufuran carry denial and the covering of received benefit together.
findings.reader_payoff: The range of examples becomes an adaptive address whose abundance does not compel assent; the majority's response is part of the scene rather than a verdict on the address.
findings.containment: The focus still plainly reports diversified examples and majority refusal, and 17:88 can remain an inimitability claim. This relation does not say every person refuses or make ingratitude replace doctrinal denial; the two kufuran facets remain compatible.

epistemic.reason: Exact focus and pericope surfaces ground the relation, and the cited channel evidence is trusted. The Qur'an-as-recitation facet is a source-semantic nomination rather than an independently reviewed lexicon facet, so that part remains bounded.

findings.title: One source, opposed reception
findings.claim: The preceding ayah gives one Qur'anic source two outcomes: healing and mercy for believers, increased loss for wrongdoers. Beside the focus's varied examples and majority refusal, that split makes the response dependent on how the audience receives the address.
findings.mechanism: The Qur'an named at 17:82 returns as the Qur'an in the focus; healing and mercy meet believers while loss meets wrongdoers. This recipient split contacts the focus's covering branch of kufuran, so the increased range of examples need not mechanically erase a resistant orientation.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's refusal becomes part of a wider account of reception: disclosure can remain one source while its effects differ with its hearers.
findings.containment: The preceding text may simply distinguish two recipient groups without asserting a general amplification law. The focus still states the majority's refusal; the contextual reading adds a receiver relation and leaves doctrinal denial available.

epistemic.reason: The exact 17:82 roots and indices and the focus return match supplied surfaces. The HFT reader identity remains legacy_unbound, so its receiver-dependent mechanism is retained as attributed evidence.

findings.title: Revelation as a retained gift

findings.mechanism: The removal verb and revealed object make the disclosure contingent; mercy and great favor name its continuation. The focus names the Qur'an and every example, then closes with kufuran, whose favor-denial facet contacts that prior gift relation and changes refusal into possible ingratitude toward retained revelation.
findings.reader_payoff: The extensive address is newly perceptible as something received and continued, not simply an available resource whose presence is owed.
findings.containment: The removal in 17:86 is conditional, not a prediction. The text does not explicitly call each example a favor, and kufuran can still carry doctrinal denial; the gift reading adds a relation without replacing either.

epistemic.reason: All five HFT root and word coordinates match the supplied 17:86-87 and focus surfaces. Because the reader identity is legacy_unbound, the gift-to-ingratitude connection remains attributed.

findings.title: From unattainable likeness to examples
findings.claim: The preceding ayah gathers humans and jinn, even with mutual support, around an attempt to bring the Qur'an's likeness; the focus then turns through every mathal for people. The adjacency makes failed external reproduction and abundant internal exemplification legible together.
findings.mechanism: The coalition, mutual backing, and impossible counterpart in 17:88 contact the focus's same-root example word and its varied presentation. A likeness no coalition can produce is followed by examples the Qur'an presents for people, shifting the sequence from a boundary on imitation to a generative mode of explanation.
findings.reader_payoff: Inimitability and exemplification become related parts of the pericope: the text that cannot be reproduced is itself presented through examples.
findings.containment: The repeated root and adjacency may be ordinary lexical recurrence, and 17:88 may stand as an inimitability statement on its own. This reading adds a generative relation without claiming the senses are identical or that it exhausts the focus.

epistemic.reason: The HFT coordinates for coalition, likeness, Qur'an, and mutual aid all match 17:88, and the focus mathal return is exact. Reader identity remains legacy_unbound, so the cross-ayah synthesis stays attributed.

findings.title: A moving proof threshold
findings.claim: After the focus records refusal, the next ayat voice a series of conditions: a spring, a garden and rivers, a divided sky or angels, then a gilded house or ascent followed by a book the audience can read. The repeated conditional form makes the admission threshold appear to move with the requested proof.
findings.mechanism: The focus's abā supplies the refusal carrier; the subsequent until-clauses and alternating requests give that refusal a changing set of conditions. Even ascent does not close the sequence, since the audience then requires a descended written object for its own reading.
findings.reader_payoff: The refusal becomes visible in the form of its requests: the evidence medium keeps changing, and the last condition reserves verification for the audience.
findings.containment: The sequence may be one rhetorical catalogue of alternatives rather than a chronologically moving threshold, and the conditions remain the audience's stated demands. The focus still reports refusal without requiring that every requester acts in bad faith.

epistemic.reason: All seven HFT coordinates match supplied roots in 17:90 and 17:93 or the focus; connections and exact text also cover 17:91-92. The HFT identity is legacy_unbound, so the threshold inference remains attributed.

findings.title: A matched messenger is refused
findings.claim: The focus directs its varied examples to people and records majority refusal. The later exchange states that people object to a human messenger, then explains that angels living on earth would receive an angel messenger; the issue becomes the recipient's relation to the medium of disclosure.
findings.mechanism: The focus's people-word is both the named beneficiary and the refusing audience. The objection to a human messenger contacts that audience, and the counterfactual matches messenger kind to inhabitant kind, so human likeness can be read as a fit that the audience itself treats as a barrier.
findings.reader_payoff: Refusal becomes a dispute about who may carry disclosure to whom, rather than a simple absence of examples.
findings.containment: The answer in 17:95 may rebut a demand for supernatural prestige without proposing a universal medium-matching principle. This addition keeps the focus's primary report intact and does not claim that all objections have one cause.

epistemic.reason: All HFT word indices and roots match the supplied 17:94-95 and focus surfaces. The human-facing branch application and broader fit inference remain attributed because the reader identity is legacy_unbound.

findings.title: Majority as prevalence, witness as measure
findings.claim: The focus gives refusal a majority scale. The pericope closes by saying that God suffices as witness and is knowledgeable of inner states and seeing of outward acts, making the majority count visible without making it the verdict on the address.
findings.mechanism: Akthar carries a numerical majority; the closing sufficiency and testimony are joined to inward knowledge and sight. That separate witness relation contacts the focus's count and shifts it from a disappointing verdict to a measure of how widespread refusal is.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish how many refuse from what counts as evidence about the message and its reception.
findings.containment: The closing witness may validate the messenger without directly commenting on majority epistemology. Akthar still means most, not all, and the contextual reading adds a measure without displacing that wording.

epistemic.reason: All HFT coordinates match the supplied 17:96 roots and the focus akthar occurrence. The reader identity is legacy_unbound, so the link between majority prevalence and evidentiary weight remains attributed.

findings.title: A responsive voice in the overlay
findings.claim: The separately added Fātiḥa verses place a first-person voice of praise, worship, dependence, and guidance-seeking beside the focus's report that most people refuse. Through the favor-denial facet of kufuran, they add a concrete response posture to the macro account of reception.
findings.mechanism: The focus's kufuran can carry denial of a benefit; 1:2 praises God, and 1:5-6 says we worship, seek help, and ask for guidance. The contact makes one supplied human response audible alongside the majority refusal, changing the contrast from a count alone to differing relations of reception.
findings.reader_payoff: The majority wording need not flatten the audience into one response; the overlay supplies a voiced posture of praise and dependence while leaving its relation to that majority open.
findings.containment: This is an analogical overlay. The supplied Fātiḥa voice is not identified as the focus's historical audience, its minority, or a direct answer to this ayah. The focus itself still reports majority refusal.

epistemic.reason: The cited Arabic is present, but no explicit cross-ayah link identifies the first-person voice with the focus audience. The response comparison is a bounded inference from the declared external overlay.
